reference.title: Useful language for showing interest
rows: I went to New York last week.
The weather was terrible – it rained every day.
Oh no! What a pity! What did you do?
We went to a show in the West End.
I lost my phone on the first day.
Really? How awful! How did you lose it?

reference.title: Showing interest
reference.text: React to good news with Wow! Great! Fantastic! and to bad news with Oh no! What a pity! How awful! Say Really? when something is surprising. Then ask a follow-up question: Did you like it? What did you do? How did you lose it? Use an ‘interested’ intonation – your voice goes up and down.

reference.title: Your last holiday – questions
reference.text: Where did you go? When did you go? Who did you go with? Where did you stay? What was it like? What was the weather like? What did you do during the day / in the evening? Did you have a good time? Did you have any problems?

tasks.context: ‘Passport, tickets, money, phone’ – It’s the mantra we always say to ourselves when we go on holiday to make sure we haven’t forgotten anything. But what happens when one of those things is suddenly missing? Last year, I went on holiday to the Alps with a group of friends. One day, we climbed a mountain – well, it wasn’t really a climb, but it was a long walk – and it took about two hours to get to the top. When we got there, we had lunch. The view was amazing – we could see the sea in the distance. We took photos and just sat in the sun for a while. Then we went down again, and when we got back to the car, I wanted to take another photo, but I couldn’t find my phone – it wasn’t in my bag. I thought ‘Oh no! It’s probably at the top of the mountain, where we had lunch.’ I decided the only thing to do was to go back up the mountain to get it, because I didn’t want to leave my phone up there. My friends said ‘OK, but you can’t go on your own’, so in the end we all went up again, which was another two hours. When we got to the top we spent about half an hour looking for the phone, but we couldn’t find it anywhere. Then it started to get colder – it was now late afternoon – so I took my jacket out of my bag, and… my phone was in my jacket pocket! I felt terrible, and really stupid! My friends were very nice about it, but they never let me forget it! (Stuart, from Exeter, UK)

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). You talk about losing things on holiday. First ask the student: Have you ever lost anything important on holiday? What was it? What happened? Did you find it? If they say no, ask about a friend or family member, or about something they lost at home. React with interest (Really? Oh no! How awful!) and ask follow-up questions in the past simple (Where were you? What did you do? How did you feel?). Then tell your story: two years ago in Rome you lost your wallet with all your money on a bus; you went to the police, you felt terrible, and the next day a woman phoned the hotel – she found it on the bus. Use short, simple past simple sentences. If the student makes a mistake with a past form (e.g. I losed, I didn’t found), repeat the correct form naturally in your reply.
exercises.goal: Tell your classmate about a time you (or someone you know) lost something important on holiday: what it was and what happened. Then listen to their story and show interest.
exercises.opener: Hi! Have you ever lost anything important on holiday?

uses didn’t / couldn’t correctly in at least one negative
reacts to the partner’s story with interest (Really? Oh no! How awful!) or asks a question in the past simple

sections.title: past simple: regular and irregular verbs

reference.title: Past simple
rows: We stayed at a hotel last summer.
I went to Turkey twice last year.
Did you stay for the weekend?

reference.text: We use the past simple to talk about finished actions that happened once or more than once in the past. The form is the same for all persons. To make the + of regular verbs add -ed. Many common verbs are irregular in +: go → went, see → saw (Irregular verbs p.164).

reference.title: Negatives and questions
reference.text: Use didn’t + infinitive for negatives and Did… + subject + infinitive for questions: I didn’t go. Did you go? Use ASI and QuASI to remember word order in questions (see 1A). was / were and could don’t use did: It wasn’t a climb. Were they happy? I couldn’t find my phone. Could you see the sea?

reference.title: Spelling rules for regular verbs
rows: add -d if the verb finishes in e

reference.why: be doesn’t use did: wasn’t / weren’t.

reference.title: -ed endings
rows: I booked a hotel. We missed our flight.
I arrived at the airport. We phoned our friends.
She invited us to stay. I needed a new passport.

reference.title: Regular past simple verbs
reference.text: The -ed ending is usually pronounced /t/ or /d/, e.g. booked, arrived. We only pronounce the e in -ed when there is a t or a d before it, e.g. wanted, ended: -ed = /ɪd/.

reference.why: Don’t pronounce the e: -ed = /ɪd/ only after t or d.

reference.title: Other holiday phrases
rows: in a hotel / at a campsite / with friends

reference.title: rent or hire?
reference.text: Rent and hire mean the same but we normally use rent for a longer period of time, e.g. you rent a flat or an apartment, and hire for a short time, e.g. you hire skis, a bike, a boat, etc. With a car you can use hire or rent.

reference.title: Adjectives
rows: What was the weather like? It was…
What was the hotel like? It was…
What was the town like? It was…
What were the people like? They were…

reference.title: General positive and negative adjectives
reference.text: Positive: great, lovely, wonderful, fantastic. Neutral: OK, not bad, all right. Negative: awful, horrible, terrible.

reference.wrong: I want to go to abroad.
reference.why: abroad is an adverb: no to.

reference.wrong: We made a lot of photos.
reference.right: We took a lot of photos.
